children: By Paul Berger
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has DP World, the Middle East's largest port operator, racing to reroute cargo around a bottleneck that once seemed improbable.

After the U.S.-Iran war effectively closed the waterway, trade at Dubai's Port of Jebel Ali-the crown jewel of DP World's global ports network-plummeted 90%, posing a challenge to the company's new chief executive, Yuvraj Narayan.

Jebel Ali serves as a gateway to the Middle East as well as a transshipment hub connecting Asia, Europe, the Americas and Africa. Lloyd's List ranked it last year as the world's ninth-busiest container port.

To keep food and other essential commodities flowing to Dubai, DP World is shifting cargoes to road and rail networks linked to ports in the Gulf of Oman, the Red Sea and as far away as Turkey. The company has also added 700 trucks to its Middle East fleet and committed $500 million to build two new port facilities on the Gulf of Oman to bypass Hormuz.

Narayan took charge of DP World in mid-February after Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem's abrupt resignation over his ties to Jeffrey Epstein. Narayan, a DP World veteran who previously served as CFO and deputy CEO, talked with The Wall Street Journal about mounting losses at Jebel Ali and whether the port can recover as a crossroads for global trade. This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity:
WSJ: What is the situation in Jebel Ali today?

Yuvraj Narayan: Jebel Ali is doing 10% of what it used to do. Every month we're not doing business, it costs us $90 million of lost profit. But DP World is a very strong company. Don't forget that our other ports and businesses around the world are doing very well. In 2025, our earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was $6.4 billion. In 2026, it will be roughly $6 billion because the balance is being made up by growth and profitability in the rest of our business. But without the war, we would have been at $7 billion-plus.
WSJ: How does Jebel Ali move forward from a situation like this?

Narayan: No single alternative to Jebel Ali exists in the Middle East. But we are finding alternate capacities and alternate routes for cargo outside Dubai. We have capacities in India. We have capacities on the east coast of Africa. We are building capacities on the Red Sea. But the cost of this is paid by the world, not by DP World.
WSJ: What do you mean?

Narayan: The cost of the whole supply chain is going up substantially. Jebel Ali used to be a gateway to the upper Gulf, a gateway to the east coast of Africa and a gateway through the Suez Canal to Europe. But today you have the Strait of Hormuz impaired. Tomorrow you will have the Red Sea impaired. The alternative routes are longer. You can double your supply-chain costs.
WSJ: Jebel Ali handled about 15 million containers a year before the war. Do you envisage a full return of cargo after Hormuz reopens?

Narayan: Absolutely. Because there aren't any alternatives. Now, it might take three months to return. But unless you create a place which gives you the same cost dynamics and the same connectivity, this will always remain a place of choice.

WSJ: DP World recently said it would build new port facilities at Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman that will act as a bypass for Hormuz. I understand DP World had the option to invest in Fujairah decades ago. Why didn't it do so then?

Narayan: I don't think there was anybody in the business of shipping who ever thought that the Strait of Hormuz will get closed for navigation one day. Now that we have seen it can happen, we need to do this to protect the Dubai ecosystem.
WSJ: Has this crisis forced DP World to consider other geopolitical crises that you assumed wouldn't happen?
Narayan: Absolutely. Look, we had this on our risk register as a very high impact item, but a very low probability item.
WSJ: So, what else is on your risk register?
Narayan: Every waterway: The Suez Canal, the Red Sea, the Panama Canal, the Malacca Straits. Eighty percent of global trade is on the marine route. I only hope sanity prevails.
